We’ve got a great chat up with my former colleague Nathaniel Rakich this morning on which threats to the integrity of the midterms are worth taking seriously (and which are overblown).

Yes and often a good example of how left vs. right is not the same as D vs. R. Ideological differences are healthy, partisanship is lame.

But you can see conspiratorial thinking about Butler and other recent violent events bubble into more "respectable" circles sometimes. Some of the more partisan D substacks are "false-flag-curious", you might say.

Yeah, this is a more common belief than I think people want to acknowledge. In part because Democrats have a bigger delta between normie/base and elite/media discourse (i.e. less tolerance for conspiratorial thinking).


Jesse Arm (@Jesse_Leg)

In our last @ManhattanInst survey, we found that 46% of today’s Democratic coalition believes “the assassination attempt against Donald Trump in July 2024 was orchestrated by his supporters to increase sympathy for him.”

Taking a deeper dive on the generic ballot vs. Trump approval in today's newsletter. Is Dems' bad brand hurting them? Turnout advantage not baked in yet? And is this year   even an outlier? Or is this all pretty normal?

Likely fairly rational behavior all-around: Democrats don't have any problem raising money, but the DNC provides a poor return on investment given current leadership. (This is the exceptionally polite version of this tweet.)


Teddy Schleifer (@teddyschleifer)

The Republican National Committee entered April with $117 million on hand.

The Democratic National Committee entered April with negative $4.4 million on hand, inclusive of debts.



— https://nitter.net/teddyschleifer/status/204635074391

Not sure it's necessarily just a sign of superior intelligence. It seems to reflect some combination of Claude's own interests, an implicit (or explicit?) goal to manage compute/bandwidth, and a trained tendency to satisfice that doesn't always match needs for power users.

This has been my experience with 4.6 too. The tell is often how quickly it accomplishes the task. It literally zips along for interesting/novel tasks. But once a project reaches a sufficient point of complexity, you sometimes have to sell it on, like, fixing annoying known bugs.

How popular is Donald Trump?. Silver Bulletin approval ratings for President Trump — and all presidents since Truman.
How popular is the Iran War? . Silver Bulletin approval ratings for the ongoing conflict.
Who’s ahead on the generic congressional ballot?. Our constantly-updating tracker of polls for the most important indicator in the race for Congress.
How much can Trump screw with the midterms? (by Eli McKown-Dawson). Doomsday scenarios are unlikely, but the realistic ones deserve more attention. A Q&A with Votebeat's Nathaniel Rakich.
How popular is Elon Musk? . Silver Bulletin favorability ratings for the world's richest man.
Can we please stop rationalizing political violence?
Yes, Virginia, redistricting is a two-player game. Democratic voters are pretty rational. For once, their leadership has been, too.
SBSQ #31: Trump is super unpopular. So why don’t Democrats have a bigger lead?. A deeper look at the generic ballot. Plus, the game theory of the automated strike zone. And more models coming soon!
The profoundly weird race for Rookie of the Year (by Joseph George). Dramatic late twists, stats versus vibes — and another test of what prediction markets really measure.
"Engagement" is a dumb metric. An algorithm doesn’t always tell you what content people truly find valuable. Plus more from my chat with Mike Solana.
“AI polls” are fake polls (by Eli McKown-Dawson). But they might be useful as something else: models.
Nuclear brinkmanship usually works. It’s also incredibly dangerous.. A small chance of a catastrophic outcome isn’t something to shrug off.

Iran is Trump's biggest political mistake. Narrow mandates and "transformative" presidencies aren’t a good political match.
